question: Debugging error test. Given #define SQ(x) x*x, what is printed by printf("%d", SQ(2+3));?
option_d: A compile-time error, because a macro cannot take an expression
explanation: The macro pastes the text 2+3 into x*x, so the compiler sees 2+3*2+3. Multiplication happens before addition, which makes 11, not 25. Remember: a macro pastes text, and the star binds tighter than the plus.
hint: Do not square 5. The parentheses are missing.
hint_3: Expand first, then do the multiplication before the addition.

question: Debugging error test. int bump(void) { static int c = 0; c = c + 1; return c; } What is printed by printf("%d", bump() + bump());?
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: The static local starts at 0 once, the first call returns 1, and the second call returns 2. Adding those return values gives 3, whichever call is evaluated first. Remember: a static local keeps its value, so two calls are not two fresh zeros.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. The static local is initialised once, not on every call.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. The first call does not return 0. One call alone is not the whole expression, and the two calls do not return the same value.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: a static local keeps its value, so two calls are not two fresh zeros.

question: Debugging error test. What is wrong with this fragment? char *p = "hi"; p[0] = 'H';
option_a: A string literal cannot be stored in a pointer at all
option_b: The program modifies a string literal, which is undefined behaviour
option_c: The only error is that H must be written in lowercase
option_d: Nothing is wrong, because a pointer to a literal is always a writable array
explanation: p points at a string literal, and writing into a literal is undefined and may crash. An array declared as char buf[] = "hi" would own a writable copy. Remember: a pointer to a literal is not a licence to write into that literal.
hint: Compare a pointer to a literal with an array that was initialised from a literal.
hint_2: The pointer initialisation is legal, and the letter case is not the fault.
hint_3: Writing through the pointer tries to change the literal itself.

question: Debugging error test. What is printed? int arr[5] = {1, 2}; printf("%d", arr[3]);
option_c: A compile-time error, because every element must be written in the initialiser
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: When an initialiser lists fewer values than the array size, the remaining elements are zero-initialised. Index 3 was not listed, so arr[3] is 0. Remember: a short brace initialiser fills the rest with zero.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. An initialiser shorter than the array does not leave the remaining elements undefined.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. Index 3 is not the first element and not the second element. A short initialiser is legal.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: a short brace initialiser fills the rest with zero.

question: Debugging error test. What happens with this fragment? if (x > 0) printf("A"); printf("B"); else printf("C");
option_a: It prints B whenever x is positive
option_b: It prints C whenever x is not positive
option_c: It is a compile-time error, because the else has no matching if
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: The if controls only the first printf, and the semicolon ends that statement. The later else therefore has no matching if, which is a compile-time error. Remember: without braces, an if owns one statement, and an else cannot follow a second statement.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. An if controls only the next statement, unless braces group several statements.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. The else is not attached to the printf of B, and the fragment does not print a fixed string. The problem appears before any run.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: without braces, an if owns one statement, and an else cannot follow a second statement.

question: Debugging error test. int n; scanf("%d", n); What is the error, assuming the intent is to read into n?
option_b: The format should be %c for an int
option_c: The address of n is not passed, so scanf receives a value instead of a place to store the input
option_d: The only error is that n must be named N
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: scanf must be given the address of n so it can store the converted input. Passing n passes a value, not a destination, which is the bug. Remember: scanf needs a pointer, so an int argument needs &.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. scanf needs a destination, not a copy of the current value.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. %d is the right format for an int. The name's case is not the fault. scanf can read an int when it is given a pointer.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: scanf needs a pointer, so an int argument needs &.

question: Debugging error test. int fact(int n) { return n * fact(n - 1); } What is wrong when fact(3) is called?
option_a: The function is missing a base case, so the recursion does not stop
option_b: C does not allow a function to call itself
option_c: The only error is that fact must return float
option_d: The call prints 6 and then returns normally
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: Every call multiplies by another call with n - 1, and there is no base case that stops at 0 or 1. The recursion continues until the stack is exhausted. Remember: a recursive function needs a base case.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. Each call makes another call with a smaller argument, and nothing says when to stop.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. C allows recursion. The return type is not the defect. The call does not complete and print 6.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: a recursive function needs a base case.

question: Debugging error test. In Java, String a = new String("bank"); String b = new String("bank"); what is the value of the expression a == b?
option_a: true, because both variables contain the same characters
option_b: false, because == compares references and these are two objects
option_c: A compile-time error, because == cannot be applied to String
option_d: true, because new always returns the interned literal
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: The == operator on references tests whether both variables point at the same object, and each new String creates a different object. The characters match, so a.equals(b) would be true, but a == b is false. Remember: for Java objects, == tests identity, and equals tests content.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. Ask whether == looks at the characters or at the object identity.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. The expression is legal. new does not return one shared interned object for these two constructions. Equal characters do not make == true here.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: for Java objects, == tests identity, and equals tests content.
